In [[algebraic geometry]], the '''motivic zeta function''' of a [[smooth algebraic variety]] <math>X</math> is the [[formal power series]]:<ref name="feynman">{{cite book |last1=Marcolli |first1=Matilde |author-link=Matilde Marcolli |title=Feynman Motives |date=2010 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=9789814304481 |page=115 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Jrix_1ORR6YC |access-date=26 April 2023}}</ref>
:<math>Z(X,t)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty [X^{(n)}]t^n</math>
Here <math>X^{(n)}</math> is the <math>n</math>-th symmetric power of <math>X</math>, i.e., the quotient of <math>X^n</math> by the action of the [[symmetric group]] <math>S_n</math>, and <math>[X^{(n)}]</math> is the class of <math>X^{(n)}</math> in the ring of motives (see below).

If the [[ground field]] is finite, and one applies the counting measure to <math>Z(X,t)</math>, one obtains the [[local zeta function]] of <math>X</math>.

If the ground field is the complex numbers, and one applies [[Euler characteristic]] with compact supports to <math>Z(X,t)</math>, one obtains <math>1/(1-t)^{\chi(X)}</math>.

== Motivic measures ==

A '''motivic measure''' is a map <math>\mu</math> from the set of finite type [[scheme (mathematics)|schemes]] over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math> to a commutative [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>A</math>, satisfying the three properties
:<math>\mu(X)\,</math> depends only on the isomorphism class of <math>X</math>,
:<math>\mu(X)=\mu(Z)+\mu(X\setminus Z)</math> if <math>Z</math> is a closed subscheme of <math>X</math>,
:<math>\mu(X_1\times X_2)=\mu(X_1)\mu(X_2)</math>.
For example if <math>k</math> is a finite field and <math>A={\mathbb Z}</math> is the ring of integers, then <math>\mu(X)=\#(X(k))</math> defines a motivic measure, the ''counting measure''.

If the ground field is the complex numbers, then Euler characteristic with compact supports defines a motivic measure with values in the integers.

The zeta function with respect to a motivic measure <math>\mu</math> is the formal power series in <math>A[[t]]</math> given by
:<math>Z_\mu(X,t)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\mu(X^{(n)})t^n</math>.

There is a ''universal motivic measure''.  It takes values in the K-ring of varieties, <math>A=K(V)</math>, which is the ring generated by the symbols <math>[X]</math>, for all varieties <math>X</math>, subject to the relations
:<math>[X']=[X]\,</math> if <math>X'</math> and <math>X</math> are isomorphic,
:<math>[X]=[Z]+[X\setminus Z]</math> if <math>Z</math> is a closed subvariety of <math>X</math>,
:<math>[X_1\times X_2]=[X_1]\cdot[X_2]</math>. 
The universal motivic measure gives rise to the motivic zeta function.

== Examples ==

Let <math>\mathbb L=[{\mathbb A}^1]</math> denote the class of the [[affine space|affine line]].

:<math>Z({\mathbb A},t)=\frac{1}{1-{\mathbb L} t}</math>

:<math>Z({\mathbb A}^n,t)=\frac{1}{1-{\mathbb L}^n t}</math>

:<math>Z({\mathbb P}^n,t)=\prod_{i=0}^n\frac{1}{1-{\mathbb L}^i t}</math>

If <math>X</math> is a smooth projective irreducible [[algebraic curve|curve]] of [[genus (curve)|genus]] <math>g</math> admitting a [[line bundle]] of degree 1, and the motivic measure takes values in a field in which <math>{\mathbb L}</math> is invertible, then 
:<math>Z(X,t)=\frac{P(t)}{(1-t)(1-{\mathbb L}t)}\,,</math> 
where <math>P(t)</math> is a polynomial of degree <math>2g</math>.  Thus, in this case, the motivic zeta function is [[rational function|rational]].  In higher dimension, the motivic zeta function is not always rational.

If <math>S</math> is a smooth [[algebraic surface|surface]] over an algebraically closed field of characteristic <math>0</math>, then the generating function for the motives of the [[Hilbert scheme]]s of <math>S</math> can be expressed in terms of the motivic zeta function by ''[[Lothar Göttsche|Göttsche's]] Formula''

:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty[S^{[n]}]t^n=\prod_{m=1}^\infty Z(S,{\mathbb L}^{m-1}t^m)</math>

Here <math>S^{[n]}</math> is the Hilbert scheme of length <math>n</math> subschemes of <math>S</math>. For the affine plane this formula gives

:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty[({\mathbb A}^2)^{[n]}]t^n=\prod_{m=1}^\infty \frac{1}{1-{\mathbb L}^{m+1}t^m}</math>

This is essentially the [[partition function (number theory)|partition function]].
